headline: Medium prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks arise from shared browser/network workflows and unverified cross-agent handoff.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can run browsers and use broad network egress, so attacker-controlled web content can reach either workflow. A also uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and B consumes web/API outputs for research, making instruction-hijack plausible even without a documented direct bridge. The pairwise path is inferred, not directly evidenced, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF either agent ingests browser-rendered content as instructions without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF A's runtime-injected MCPs or B's API-fed research outputs are treated as trusted text, attacker prompts can steer actions.
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following from web content.
Add provenance tags to browser-sourced text before reuse.
Require a human review step for any tool-triggering prompt.
Restrict MCP/tool invocation to allowlisted commands.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance filtering.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches session history, project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, and provider auth data; B touches financial reports, papers, datasets, logs, and execution traces. Both have broad network egress and API access, so sensitive material could leave the local environment if either agent forwards context or files to third-party services. No shared workspace is documented, so this is inferred rather than directly observed.
conditions: IF A forwards session history or provider auth prompts to external APIs, leakage occurs.
IF B uploads logs, traces, or datasets to model backends by default, leakage occurs.
mitigations: Redact secrets before any API call.
Separate credentials from working directories.
Turn off upload of logs and traces by default.
Use per-agent network allowlists.
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters on outbound prompts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A supports multiple instances with per-installation session scope and writes to local config/plugin paths; B supports multiple instances and writes to log/. The profiles do not show a shared writable directory or overlapping mutable resource, so a direct write conflict is not established. The main risk is limited to local coordination mistakes, not a proven default collision.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable workspace, file clobbering becomes possible.
IF an orchestrator maps A's config paths and B's log directory into one shared volume, conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Mount A and B on distinct volumes.
Avoid concurrent writes to shared git state.
Use file locks for any shared artifact.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can produce code, docs, and session-derived outputs; B is a research automation agent that can act on papers, datasets, and logs. If B treats A's output as authoritative, errors can cascade from A's unverified content into B's downstream research actions. The profiles show a plausible handoff but no verification barrier, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text or code without verification, errors can propagate.
IF A's outputs are used as facts for B's research or automation steps, downstream mistakes can compound.
mitigations: Require source citations before B acts on A's output.
Insert a verification step between agents.
Limit B to read-only evaluation of A's artifacts.
Flag low-confidence claims from A.
requires-engineering: add structured handoff schemas with validation.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles provider authentication data and installation identifiers; B handles financial reports, competition datasets, and logs. Both are docs-only and open-source, but B's Azure/OpenAI/LiteLLM/Kaggle API usage plus A's provider-auth handling creates a plausible retention and residency mismatch if the same regulated data class is routed through both. No direct residency guarantee is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF EU personal data or regulated financial data is routed through B's external APIs, residency/compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF A stores provider auth prompts alongside project data, retention policy mismatches can arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents.
Review API vendor residency terms before use.
Shorten log retention to the minimum needed.
Separate auth prompts from content data.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing by data class.
